acreFoot.def: The water it takes to cover one acre one foot deep, about 326,000 gallons.

et.def: Water that leaves a field as vapor, from the soil and through the crop's leaves.

et0.def: How much water a standard grass field would use in this weather, the starting point for crop water needs.

worst1in5.def: Your average profit in the 4 worst years out of the last 20.

frontier.def: The set of plans where you cannot get more average profit without doing worse in bad years.

soilScore.def: A 0 to 100 score for how much a rotation builds soil: legumes, living roots, residue, low tillage, and variety.

shadowPrice.def: What one more acre-foot is worth to you, in extra profit per acre.

grace.def: NASA twin satellites that weigh changes in water stored underground by measuring tiny shifts in Earth's gravity.

power.def: NASA's daily weather records for any spot on Earth, built from satellites and weather models.

fallow.def: Land left unplanted and unwatered for a season or a year.

rotation.def: The order of crops you grow on the same field over the seasons.

why.satVsGround2: Satellites measure every field and every aquifer the same way, every month, so we can compare places and years. We use satellites to see the whole region, and ask you to check the numbers against your own meters.

method.idea: We treat a farm like an investment portfolio. Each crop rotation is an asset. Water is a hard budget that must hold in every year, and soil health is a minimum standard, like an ESG screen. Using 20 past years as possible futures, we find the mix of rotations that best balances average profit against profit in the worst 1-in-5 years.
method.formulasIntro: w_i is the share of your acres in rotation i. Each past year s gives every rotation a profit and a water need. ρ is your risk setting from 0 to 1.

f.objective: What we maximize: a blend of worst-years profit and average profit, weighted by your risk setting.
f.profit: Profit of the whole farm in year s is the share-weighted profit of each rotation.
f.water: The water budget must hold in every one of the 20 years, not just on average.
f.soil: The soil score must meet your minimum, shares add up to your whole farm, and no rotation goes above your limit.
f.cvar: Worst 1-in-5 years: the average of the 4 lowest years out of 20. In finance this is the negative of CVaR at 80%.
f.shadow: Water value: how much the best plan improves if you had 0.1 more acre-feet per acre.
f.et: Crop water need from NASA POWER weather (FAO-56), less effective rain, divided by irrigation efficiency.
f.sharpe: Sharpe ratio: extra profit over fallow for each dollar of year-to-year swing.
f.sortino: Sortino ratio: the same, but only years that fall below the fallow average count as risk.
f.diversification: Diversification benefit: how much less the plan swings than its rotations would on their own, because they do not all have bad years together.

stepsList: Build 20 scenarios, one per year from 2005 to 2024, each with that year's weather and prices.
For each rotation and year, compute profit per acre and applied water per acre.
List every mix of the 5 rotations in 5% steps: 10,626 mixes.
For each mix, compute its profit in every year, its average, its worst 1-in-5 years, its highest-year water, and its soil score.
Drop every mix that breaks your water budget in any year, falls below your soil minimum, or goes over a rotation limit.
From the mixes left, mark the efficient frontier: mixes no other mix beats on both average and worst years.
Pick the frontier mix with the best score for your risk setting. Repeat with 0.1 AF more water to price water.
sourceRows: University of Arizona WRRC, Pinal AMA water report (measured applied water)
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension, Pinal County crop budgets
Team rubric on the USDA NRCS soil-health principles; tillage passes from the University of Arizona crop budgets
method.heatTitle: {{a}} and {{b}} move together least (r = {{v}}), so mixing them spreads risk
method.heatSub: How each pair of rotations' yearly profits moved together over {{from}} to {{to}}.
method.heatHow1: 1 means two rotations always rose and fell together. 0 means no link. Below 0 means one tends to do well when the other does badly.
method.heatHow2: Mixing rotations with low numbers is what protects you in bad years, just like a diversified investment portfolio.
method.backtestIntro: To check the method is not just fitting the past, we picked plans using only 2005 to 2014, then scored them on 2015 to 2024, which the model never saw. Same water and soil limits as your settings.
method.scenariosIntro: Every past year for your suggested plan and your current plan. Download it to check our math in a spreadsheet.
method.limitsTitle: What this tool does not do
limits: It does not know your fields. Soil, wells, and contracts differ from farm to farm.
It assumes the next years look like some mix of the last 20. A new kind of year is possible.
It does not model pests, diseases, labor, or the cost of switching equipment.
Shares move in 5% steps, so the best plan between steps can differ slightly.

method.whyRisk: Classic portfolio theory measures risk by variance: how far each year's profit lands from the average. That treats a great year as risk, the same as a bad one, and it favors plans that barely move, like leaving most fields fallow. A farmer is hurt by bad years, not good ones, so we measure risk by your worst 1-in-5 years instead.

risk.intro: Three standard portfolio ratios, comparing each plan with simply leaving fields fallow ({{fallow}} per acre on average). Higher is better for all three.
risk.caption: Risk ratios, suggested plan vs. your current plan

method.flowIntro: Weather sets each year's crop water need, budgets and prices set each year's profit, and together they make the past years the optimizer tests. Groundwater is context; measured water use on Pinal farms checks our water model.

flow.title: How data flows into your plan
flow.desc: NASA POWER weather sets crop water need per year. USDA NASS prices and University of Arizona crop budgets set profit per year. Both make the past-year scenarios, which the optimizer uses to pick your plan. NASA GRACE groundwater gives regional context. Measured applied water on Pinal farms (University of Arizona WRRC report) checks our water model.

method.unitsNote: Profit in the data leaves out buying water; the tool takes off your water price ({{c}} per acre-foot) times the water applied. Water is applied irrigation water at 75% efficiency.

soilRubric.intro: Each rotation gets up to 20 points on five parts, and the soil score is their sum (0 to 100). Four parts follow the USDA NRCS soil-health principles; the fifth counts nitrogen from legumes.
soilRubric.caption: Soil-score rubric: each part, the NRCS principle it follows, and each rotation's points with the reason.
soilRubric.reviewed: An agronomist has not reviewed these scores yet; check them with a local expert.

tour.plan: Look at the suggested mix and the four numbers under it, compared with your current plan cut back to fit your water.
tour.tradeoffs: Move the water slider and watch the choices shrink; switch to Profit vs. soil to see what a higher soil score costs, and turn on the classic portfolio theory comparison.
tour.stress: Pick 2020 or 2022 and see how both plans would have done in that one hard year.
tour.method: Audit every formula, the sensitivity check, the backtest, and download the scenario table.

about.problem: Central Arizona farms lost their Colorado River water in just three years. Farmers now have to choose what to plant on less water, through hot summers, without knowing which years will be bad.
approach: Soil health comes first: you set a minimum soil score and no plan goes below it. Scores follow the USDA NRCS soil-health principles, and you choose which soil goals count.
Resilience to weather and water: every plan must fit your water in each of {{n}} past years of weather, including the hottest, not just on average.
Then the investor's method: we weigh how much a plan earns in its {{k}} worst years against its average, and show the trade-off openly.
about.realIntro: Where every input comes from. Each one carries its own flag, and all the data behind the plan is real.
about.siText: Our team used SI to help design, debug, and modify the application. SI helped us rapidly prototype and iterate on our ideas.
